newsitem.title: GERMANY: Solidarity tax must be maintained-German president.
newsitem.headline: Solidarity tax must be maintained-German president.

text.p: The unpopular surcharge raised to aid east Germany, the solidarity tax, would remain a necessity over a longer period, Germany's president Roman Herzog said in a newspaper interview on Sunday.

"The economy, and the development of the economy, in the former east German states is not yet self-sufficient and the eastern German states will need our support for a while yet," Herzog told the Sunday newspaper Bild am Sonntag.
At the same time, junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) -- who have staked their political survival on tax cuts -- called for the speedy abolition of the surcharge.
FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhard told the Sunday newspaper Welt am Sonntag that the solidarity tax was not at the core of tax reform, but was the starting point.

Shortly before Christmas, Chancellor Kohl's three-party ruling coalition agreed to cut the solidarity surcharge to 5.5 percent on January 1, 1998, but so far the coalition has failed to find a way to finance the reduction.
Herzog went on to say that an increase in value-added tax looked unavoidable in a European context, and said that tax on pensions should not be considered a taboo subject.
The chairman of the DGB trade unions association, Dieter Schulte, called for an equitable reform of Germany's taxes, which would favour those groups who have been hit hardest by previous tax regimes.
Schulte said on German radio that the DGB would not support any tax reform which was financed by introducing taxes on Sunday work or night shifts.
